nameStory: The "crane's-bill" name comes from the plant's distinctive seed pods, which have a long, pointed beak that looks just like a crane's bill! When the seeds ripen, this "bill" splits open dramatically and flings the seeds away from the parent plant. The "Carolina" part refers to where this little geranium was first scientifically described, though it actually grows throughout much of North America.
description: Carolina crane's-bill is a small, low-growing annual wildflower that often goes unnoticed until you get down close to examine it. This modest plant typically grows 6-18 inches tall with delicate, deeply-lobed leaves that look almost lacy. Its tiny pink or white flowers are just a quarter-inch across, but the real showstopper is the long, needle-like seed pod that gives the plant its memorable name. You'll often find it growing as a somewhat weedy groundcover in disturbed areas.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: The unmistakable long, pointed seed pod (the "crane's bill") extends up to an inch long and splits into five curling segments when ripe, creating a small explosion that scatters seeds

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pink or white flowers, usually less than a quarter-inch across, with five rounded petals that often have darker pink veins; flowers appear in small clusters

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided, palm-shaped leaves that feel slightly fuzzy and are cut into 5-7 narrow segments, giving them a delicate, lacy appearance

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, sprawling annual that forms small mats or patches, with stems that often have a reddish tinge and feel slightly sticky when touched

habitat: Look for Carolina crane's-bill in disturbed soils, along roadsides, in gardens, fields, and waste areas throughout New England. It thrives in sunny to partially shaded spots with well-drained soil and doesn't mind poor or sandy conditions. You'll often find it growing alongside other weedy annuals in areas that have been recently disturbed by human activity.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge early and begin developing their characteristic deeply-lobed leaves. Early flowers may appear by late spring in warmer areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with tiny pink or white flowers appearing continuously. The distinctive crane's-bill seed pods begin forming and can be seen alongside flowers.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and the dramatic "explosion" of the crane's-bill pods occurs, flinging seeds several feet away. Plants begin to decline as cooler weather arrives.
seasonality.winter: As an annual, plants die completely, leaving only seeds in the soil to sprout the following spring.

funFact: The crane's-bill seed pod is actually a tiny catapult! When the seeds ripen, the five sections of the "bill" suddenly curl backward with such force that they can launch seeds up to 15 feet away from the parent plant, making this one of nature's most efficient seed-scattering mechanisms.
confusionNotes: Carolina crane's-bill is often confused with other small geraniums, especially Herb Robert, but Carolina crane's-bill has much smaller flowers and less dissected leaves. Remember: if the flowers are tiny (less than a quarter-inch) and the plant looks weedy and low-growing, it's likely Carolina crane's-bill rather than the showier wild geranium.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse these wild geraniums with the colorful potted "geraniums" sold at garden centers, which are actually pelargoniums from South Africa. True geraniums like Carolina crane's-bill are hardy native wildflowers, while garden "geraniums" are tender tropical plants that can't survive New England winters.
compareHints: Among New England's crane's-bills, Carolina crane's-bill has the smallest flowers - much tinier than the showy inch-wide blooms of wild geranium or the medium-sized flowers of Herb Robert. Its leaves are also less finely divided than Herb Robert's ferny foliage, and it lacks the strong musky smell that makes Herb Robert so distinctive when crushed.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wild geranium stands out from its cranesbill cousins by its substantial size, soft pink flowers, and preference for rich woodlands.
Among New England's wild geraniums, Herb Robert is the most delicate and lacy-looking, with much more finely divided leaves than the larger Wild Geranium.
Among New England's crane's-bills, bloody crane's-bill stands out for its deeply divided leaves that are cut almost to the base, creating very narrow segments.
Among New England's crane's-bills, rock crane's-bill is unique for its low, mat-forming growth and intensely fragrant leaves - most others grow more upright and have much less scented foliage.
Northern cranesbill is much smaller and more delicate than wild geranium, with tiny lavender flowers instead of large pink ones.
Thunberg's Geranium is much smaller and more delicate than our common Wild Geranium, with more finely divided leaves and smaller flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, meadow crane's-bill is one of the largest and most robust, forming much bigger clumps than most relatives.

Among New England's crane's-bills, dusky crane's-bill is unique for its nearly black flowers with backward-curved petals - our native wild geranium has pink flowers that face upward, while Herb Robert has small bright pink flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, dove's-foot stands out for its exceptionally soft, velvety leaf texture and low, mat-forming growth habit.
Among New England's crane's-bills, this is one of the tiniest and most easily overlooked.
Purple-vein geranium stands out from other New England geraniums primarily by its bright blue flowers - most other species have pink, white, or purple blooms.

Among New England's crane's-bills, cut-leaved crane's-bill stands out for having the most finely divided leaves - while wild geranium has broader, less deeply cut leaves and Herb Robert has more triangular leaf segments, cut-leaved crane's-bill looks almost feathery.
Among New England's crane's-bills, little-robin is the tiniest - much smaller than wild geranium or Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Long-stalked stands out for its exceptionally long flower stalks and deeply dissected leaves.

Richardson's geranium differs from New England's common wild geranium by having paler flowers with more prominent dark veining, perfectly straight (not curved) seed beaks, and more finely divided leaf segments.
Wood crane's-bill differs from our native wild geranium by having more deeply dissected leaves and typically stronger purple coloring with more prominent petal veining.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Siberian Crane's-bill would be one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
